item.title: Teaching Assistant — Robot Mechanics & Control
item.description:
The lab

Northeastern, Sep 2024 – Apr 2025. A MathWorks-funded, cost-optimised robotics curriculum built around the PincherX-100 — a four-DOF arm with Dynamixel servos, cheap enough to put a cell in front of every student group.

One lab cell. Overhead camera for marker-based pose estimation, side camera for recording runs, and a marked workspace the arm has to localise targets within.

The teaching problem with a shared robot cell is that students have to write code that drives real motors, and a sign error in an IK solver drives the gripper into the table. So the framework is built in two tiers: everything runs in simulation first, and the same student code moves to hardware unchanged.

Analytical IK

Rather than hand students a numerical solver, the arm’s kinematics are solved in closed form — the geometry is simple enough that it’s tractable by hand, which is the point of the exercise.

Strip the fixed wrist-to-end-effector transform off the target pose, then:

theta1 = atan2(y4, x4);                                  % waist, from the base projection

D = (r^2 + z_eff^2 - L2^2 - L3^2) / (2 * L2 * L3);       % law of cosines
if abs(D) > 1
    error('Target is out of reach — no IK solution.');
end
theta3 = atan2(sqrt(1 - D^2), D);                        % elbow-up branch

alpha  = atan2(z_eff, r);
beta   = atan2(L3*sin(theta3), L2 + L3*cos(theta3));
theta2 = -(alpha + beta);

theta234 = atan2(-T_04(3,1), -T_04(3,2));                % wrist from the rotation block
theta4   = theta234 - theta2 - theta3;

Link lengths L2 = 0.1059, L3 = 0.1, shoulder height 0.0931 m. Two things worth noting pedagogically: the abs(D) > 1 check means an unreachable target fails loudly with a message rather than returning a complex angle that silently becomes garbage downstream, and the elbow-up branch is selected explicitly — students have to decide which of the two solutions they want rather than discovering the arm occasionally folds the other way.

The safety gate

This is the piece that makes remote hardware execution viable. Every commanded configuration goes through set_joint_pos, which refuses it on two grounds:

  • Joint limits — each of the four angles checked against the URDF’s range.
  • Table collision — forward kinematics is run to px100/ee_gripper_link and the resulting world-frame z is compared against a floor threshold.

The second check is the important one. Joint limits alone don’t protect anything — every individual joint can be in range while the arm as a whole is below the table. Running FK on the commanded pose before sending it to the servos catches the combination, and it means a student’s broken IK produces a refusal instead of a repair ticket.

Perception

Target positions come from markers rather than hardcoded coordinates, so the arm has to actually localise the object. Calibrated overhead camera, with intrinsics measured for the cell:
Focal length 1216.56, 1216.90 px
Principal point 645.49, 363.51 px
Radial distortion −0.4428, 0.2414
Resolution 1280 × 720

Markers are assigned by role — ID 0 is the base frame, ID 1 sits on the object to pick, IDs 2–5 are candidate drop locations. The base marker is what makes the whole thing work: detections arrive in camera coordinates, and composing through the base tag puts the target in the robot’s frame without anyone measuring where the camera is. Tag sizes differ deliberately (2 cm for base and drop, 1 cm for the pick marker) so a small marker can sit on top of a small object without occluding it.

Combined with the IK above, the cell reaches ±2.5 mm end-effector precision.

Motor control

Students also get underneath the position controller. set_dynamixel_pid writes straight to the Dynamixel control table — addresses 80, 82 and 84 for the D, I and P gains — and pid_checking.m is a step-response harness: command the waist joint from 0 to 1 rad, log actual position against time, change a gain, run it again.

Reading an encoder trace that overshoots and oscillates, then watching it settle after raising D, is a more durable lesson about PID than a Bode plot. Gripper control is similarly concrete: open and closed are literally encoder counts 2573 and 2048.

Sim-to-real

The two entry points are deliberately near-identical:

Simulation Hardware
Script Visual.m pick_place.m
Target poses set in-script detected from markers
Obstacles toggleable the real table
Output Simscape animation recorded video of the run

Both drive the same ikpincher100, the same set_joint_pos safety gate, and the same URDF — px100.urdf with eight STL meshes, imported through importrobot for simulation and shipped alongside a Simscape model (px100_simple.slx) for the dynamics exercises. The simulation path adds approach waypoints above the pick and drop poses, so students meet the idea that a straight line between two valid poses is not necessarily a valid path.

Library loading is handled per-platform (Windows, Linux, macOS) in init_robot.m, which sounds trivial and is the kind of thing that otherwise eats the first hour of every lab session.

What the framework ships

File Role
init_robot.m Dynamixel SDK bringup, URDF import, robot struct
ikpincher100.m Closed-form inverse kinematics
set_joint_pos.m Joint-limit and table-collision safety gate
get_joint_pos.m Bulk encoder read, counts → radians
get_pick_and_place_position.m Marker detection and base-frame transform
pick_place.m / Visual.m Hardware and simulation task entry points
pid_checking.m, set_dynamixel_pid.m Servo gain tuning exercise
closeGripper.m Gripper open/close
px100.urdf, *.stl, px100_simple.slx Robot model and Simscape dynamics

item.title: Graduate Research Assistant
item.description:
Energy-Aware Collaborative Exploration for a UAV–UGV Team

Multi-Agent Robotics and Autonomy Lab, Northeastern University.

Er, Juttu, Yazıcıoğlu — submitted to IROS 2026. arXiv:2603.22507 · code

Hardware run at 10× speed, terminating once the team passes 95% coverage. The full-resolution video is attached to the release.

The problem

A quadrotor has maybe fifteen minutes of flight time. That is the binding constraint on aerial exploration, and the usual fix — fly back to a fixed charging station — wastes an increasing fraction of each tour on transit as the frontier moves away.

So the ground robot becomes the charging station. The UAV flies a sequence of energy-bounded tours, each ending in a rendezvous where it lands on a platform mounted on the UGV and recharges. The UGV explores the ground in the meantime, so the recharge leg is not dead time for the team.

The pairing is genuinely complementary in both directions: the UGV drives through passages the UAV cannot fly, and the UAV reaches elevated structure the UGV cannot climb. In the test arenas neither robot alone achieves full coverage.

Planning

Exploration targets are sampled into a density-aware layered PRM spanning air and ground, and each pair of tours comes from solving coupled orienteering problems — maximise information gain subject to a shared rendezvous time budget.

The coupling lives in one line. Candidate aerial targets are scored

score = info_gain · exp(−λ · t_ugv_path)

so the UAV’s goal is its information gain discounted by how far the UGV has to drive to get underneath it. A target rich in unexplored volume but far from any drivable ground is worth less than a mediocre one the UGV can already reach, because the rendezvous has to be feasible or the tour strands the drone. Four hard gates sit on top: a candidate is rejected if its gain is ≤ 10, if it has no ground twin, if the vertical corridor between the aerial node and its twin is not collision-free, or if that twin is unreachable in the ground graph.

The orienteering problems are solved with GRASP with path relinking — randomised greedy insertion by score-to-time ratio, 2-opt and swap-insert local search, then path relinking between elite solutions. Every move is validated against the roadmap, with infinite time-matrix entries for non-edges, so no tour can shortcut off a collision-checked edge.

Coordination

A 20 Hz state machine runs the mission: initial takeoff, a 360° scan to seed the map, then plan → execute → rendezvous → recharge until the planner latches completion at 97% coverage. Both tours execute simultaneously — the UAV gets its whole path at once, the UGV gets waypoints dispatched one at a time through move_base.

Three details that only show up once it runs on hardware:

Landing alignment. Each UGV waypoint is given a yaw pointing at the next one, for smooth navigation — except the last, which instead inherits the UAV’s final orientation. That is what squares the landing platform up with the descending drone.

Touchdown debouncing. Touchdown is confirmed only after the UAV holds below 0.75 m for two consecutive seconds. A single noisy altitude sample would otherwise end a tour early, mid-descent.

Replanning has to be joint. If the UAV replans around an obstacle during execution, the coordinator cancels the UGV’s active goal and recomputes both tours. The tours are coupled through a shared rendezvous — replanning one in isolation silently breaks the guarantee that the drone can reach the ground robot before its budget runs out.

Shared mapping

Mapping is bidirectional, planning is not: the UGV contributes Velodyne scans and odometry, and the planner runs in the UAV’s process, projecting the aerial roadmap down to the ground and publishing both tours. There is no second planner on the rover.

One necessary piece of bookkeeping: the UGV’s own footprint is erased from the occupancy map before its scans are injected. Without that the rover carves a moving phantom obstacle through the roadmap it is itself driving on.

Stack

C++ / ROS Noetic / Gazebo 11, OctoMap for occupancy mapping, gmapping for the 2D ground map, move_base with TEB for UGV navigation, B-spline trajectory generation and time-optimal reparameterisation on the UAV side. The UAV autonomy stack extends CERLAB-UAV-Autonomy (CMU); the UGV packages derive from the AgileX scout_ros family.

Benchmarks compare the method against a single-UAV ablation and a sequential baseline, selected as drop-in planner variants at configure time.

item.title: Brakes & Testing Head — BAJA SAE Off-Road Racing
item.description:
Overview

Role: Brakes and Testing Head
Team: Off-Road Racing Team — NIT Jalandhar
Duration: Jan 2017 – May 2019

  • Led end-to-end development of high-performance ATV brake systems.
  • Built India’s lightest ATV for BAJA SAE 2019.
  • Achieved 4th fastest ATV at BAJA SAE Illinois 2017.
  • Delivered robust braking under extreme off-road and endurance conditions.

Full Lifecycle Mechanical Design

  • Concept to CAD: Designed floating brake calipers and dual-rotor configurations in Catia V5.
  • Simulation & Analysis: Validated all designs using ANSYS 16.0 (thermal & static structural).
  • Prototyping & Testing: Built physical test setups using Arduino, load cells, and sensors.
  • DFM & Machining: Translated CAD into manufacturable parts using CNC machining and lathe operations.

Brake Caliper Design & Simulation

Developed and validated a custom floating brake caliper to suit the geometry of a compact, lightweight ATV with extreme off-road use cases.

  • Designed from scratch in Catia V5 to match suspension and rotor configurations
  • Performed FEA-based stress testing in ANSYS to validate mechanical strength under peak braking loads
  • Conducted iterative simulations to minimize deflection and ensure even brake pad wear
  • Assembly designed with DFM principles, ease of maintenance

CAD Exploded View

ANSYS FEA Analysis

Structural & Thermal Analysis (FEA)

Rear Brake Rotor

  • Conducted transient thermal analysis for heat dissipation during prolonged braking.
  • Used vented profiles to reduce thermal hotspots and fade.

*Rear Rotor — Static Structural FEA *

Front Brake Rotor

  • Combined aluminum core with SS420 stainless steel coating for weight and heat resistance.
  • Optimized spoke pattern for mechanical integrity with minimal mass.

Brake Pedal Design & Validation

  • Designed and analyzed pedal assembly with custom mount.
  • Validated force distribution using FEA and real-time load cell logging.

Prototyping, Fabrication & Machining

  • Designed parts for machinability and DFM — ensured tolerances for hydraulic caliper alignment.
  • Utilized CNC, lathe, and conventional machining techniques for part manufacturing.
  • Fabricated and tested prototypes under simulated track conditions.
  • Assembled and field-tested brake components on the actual ATV chassis.

Experimental Testing

  • Developed a custom rig using Arduino Uno, LDR, and load cell sensors to measure:
    • Acceleration during braking
    • Pedal force vs stopping distance
    • Response time


On-field brake performance testing with Arduino sensor rig

Tools & Skills

  • CAD: Catia V5, SolidWorks
  • Simulation: ANSYS (Thermal, Structural), FEA, hand calculations
  • Prototyping: CNC, lathe, drilling, aluminum fabrication
  • Testing: Arduino, load cells, custom rigs
  • Design for Manufacturing (DFM)
  • Material Selection: Aluminum, SS420, brake pad composites
  • Team Leadership & Documentation

Outcomes

  • Reduced brake system weight by 40%.
  • Increased thermal capacity and structural durability.
  • Enabled modular swap-out of brake parts for different terrains.
  • Competitive performance in national/international SAE racing events.
